speaker_role: former admissions officer (University of Pennsylvania; also worked in admissions at University of Toronto)
commercial_incentive: none evident stated in transcript (podcast-style interview, no service pitch heard)
key_insights: At Penn she read about 1,300 files/year at ~15 minutes each, spending roughly 5 of those minutes on the activities grid, which was the second thing reviewed after grades/rigor/test scores.
Each application section, including activities, was scored 1-9; most students scored 5-6, a 7-8 was rare and made her likely to advocate for admission, and she never gave a 9.
She looked for 3-4 years of committed involvement, rising to a real leadership role by senior year, and achievements that extended beyond the high school itself.

Most students' listed activities were authentic, but disconnects showed up when time claims seemed implausible (e.g., 40 hrs/week of activities) or when major achievements were never corroborated by teacher recommendation letters.
Some public/private university systems (e.g., University of Toronto for most programs) don't weigh extracurriculars at all and admit almost purely on grades, unlike the US holistic model.

Activities chosen purely to 'look good' rather than reflecting genuine interest read as inauthentic and don't strengthen a file; authenticity and internal consistency across essays/letters/activities matter more than checking boxes.

AI-generated or overly polished work stands out as suspicious mainly when it doesn't 'hang together' with the rest of the file (e.g., a middling student suddenly submitting a phenomenal, grad-student-level project).

Advises listing activities most-to-least important/time-committed (not chronologically), using sentence fragments to pack in detail, and writing about one's specific role rather than describing the activity itself, since admissions officers won't research unfamiliar activities or click links.
specific_numbers_or_facts: At Penn: ~1,300 applications read per year, ~15 minutes per file, ~30 files/day, ~5 minutes spent on the activity list per file (interviewee).
Penn scored each application section 1-9; most activity lists scored 5-6, 7-8 was rare, 9 was never given (interviewee).
Common App activities section has 10 slots; interviewee says most admissions offices meaningfully weight only roughly the first 5.
University of Toronto only considered extracurriculars for engineering and business programs during her time there; other programs admitted almost solely on grades (interviewee).
References a blog called 'Applying Sideways,' written by a former MIT admissions officer around 2013, as still-relevant advice to follow genuine interests over what looks good.
notable_or_distinctive: Gives an unusually granular inside view of real file-reading mechanics (time per section, 1-9 scoring, why only the first ~5 activity slots get real attention) rather than generic tips, plus concrete anecdotes (a student who rewrote her state's driver's-ed manual, a student who talked his way into a DC think-tank internship) illustrating what stands out.
reliability_notes: Single ex-officer's personal recollections and Penn-specific practices from some years ago; auto-caption transcript has minor garbling but is largely clear; no outside verification of the anecdotes or the claimed 1-9 scoring scale's continued use today.
